claim: Kinesins are a superfamily of microtubule (MT)-based molecular motors that play important roles in cellular functions such as mitosis, cell motility, and intracellular transport.
source: Kinesins are a superfamily of microtubule (MT)-based molecular motors that play important roles in cellular functions such as mitosis, cell motility, and intracellular transport (Vale, 2003; Hirokawa et al., 2009; Klinman and Holzbaur, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Vale, 2003; Hirokawa et al., 2009; Klinman and Holzbaur, 2018).

claim: Kinesins are categorised into 14 sub-classes (kinesin-1 to kinesin-14) by motor domain conservation.
source: Kinesins are categorised into 14 sub-classes (kinesin-1 to kinesin-14 [Lawrence et al., 2004]) by motor domain conservation and within these sub-classes individual family members (a total of 45 'KIF' or 'Kif' genes in humans and mice respectively) have a wide range of functional characteristics and biological roles (Vale, 2003; Miki et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lawrence et al., 2004.

claim: There are a total of 45 'KIF' or 'Kif' genes in humans and mice respectively.
source: Kinesins are categorised into 14 sub-classes (kinesin-1 to kinesin-14 [Lawrence et al., 2004]) by motor domain conservation and within these sub-classes individual family members (a total of 45 'KIF' or 'Kif' genes in humans and mice respectively) have a wide range of functional characteristics and biological roles (Vale, 2003; Miki et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vale, 2003 and Miki et al., 2001.

claim: Dysfunction of kinesin family members has been implicated in a number of pathological conditions.
source: Dysfunction of kinesin family members has been implicated in a number of pathological conditions (Hirokawa et al., 2010; Mandelkow and Mandelkow, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hirokawa et al., 2010 and Mandelkow and Mandelkow, 2002.

claim: The kinesin motor domain converts the chemical energy of ATP binding and hydrolysis into mechanical force.
source: The kinesin motor domain is the MT-binding engine that drives these activities, converting the chemical energy of ATP binding and hydrolysis into mechanical force.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of kinesin motor domain function.

claim: A subset of kinesin superfamily members, including kinesin-2s, −3s, −8s, and −12s, are sequestered by kinesin-binding protein (KBP).
source: Recently, it has been demonstrated that a subset of kinesin superfamily members, including kinesin-2s, −3 s, −8 s, and −12 s, are sequestered by kinesin-binding protein (KBP; KIF1BP; KIAA1279), which inhibits MT track attachment by their motor domains and, thus, blocks their MT-related functions (Wozniak et al., 2005; Kevenaar et al., 2016; Alves et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wozniak et al., 2005; Kevenaar et al., 2016; Alves et al., 2010.

claim: KBP inhibits MT track attachment by kinesin motor domains and blocks their MT-related functions.
source: Recently, it has been demonstrated that a subset of kinesin superfamily members, including kinesin-2s, −3 s, −8 s, and −12 s, are sequestered by kinesin-binding protein (KBP; KIF1BP; KIAA1279), which inhibits MT track attachment by their motor domains and, thus, blocks their MT-related functions (Wozniak et al., 2005; Kevenaar et al., 2016; Alves et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wozniak et al., 2005; Kevenaar et al., 2016; Alves et al., 2010.

claim: KBP is expressed in multiple human tissues including brain and heart.
source: KBP is expressed in multiple human tissues including brain and heart (Wozniak et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wozniak et al., 2005.

claim: Mutations in the KBP have been identified as causing autosomal recessive Goldberg-Shprintzen syndrome (GOSHS).
source: Mutations in the KBP have been identified as causing autosomal recessive Goldberg-Shprintzen syndrome (GOSHS) (Brooks et al., 2005; Dafsari et al., 2015; Valence et al., 2013; Salehpour et al., 2017), which presents as congenital facial dysmorphia, nervous system pathology, and dysfunction and heart defects (Tanaka et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brooks et al., 2005; Dafsari et al., 2015; Valence et al., 2013; Salehpour et al., 2017.

claim: Goldberg-Shprintzen syndrome presents as congenital facial dysmorphia, nervous system pathology, and dysfunction and heart defects.
source: Mutations in the KBP have been identified as causing autosomal recessive Goldberg-Shprintzen syndrome (GOSHS) (Brooks et al., 2005; Dafsari et al., 2015; Valence et al., 2013; Salehpour et al., 2017), which presents as congenital facial dysmorphia, nervous system pathology, and dysfunction and heart defects (Tanaka et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tanaka et al., 1993.

claim: KBP gene copy number has been recently reported as predictive in paediatric neuroblastoma prognosis.
source: In addition, KBP gene copy number has been recently reported as predictive in paediatric neuroblastoma prognosis, prompting its suggestion as a drug target (Suo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Suo et al., 2018.

claim: KBP was originally identified as a kinesin-3-binding partner that modulated its mitochondrial transport function.
source: KBP was originally identified as a kinesin-3-binding partner that modulated its mitochondrial transport function (Wozniak et al., 2005); however, KBP has since been shown to interact with a subset of other kinesin family members to regulate diverse cellular processes including mitosis (Brouwers et al., 2017; Malaby et al., 2019), spermatogenesis (Lehti et al., 2015), and neuronal differentiation, growth, and cargo distribution (Alves et al., 2010; Lyons et al., 2008; Drévillon et al., 2013; Drerup et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2019; Hirst et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wozniak et al., 2005.

claim: KBP interacts with a subset of other kinesin family members to regulate diverse cellular processes including mitosis, spermatogenesis, and neuronal differentiation, growth, and cargo distribution.
source: KBP was originally identified as a kinesin-3-binding partner that modulated its mitochondrial transport function (Wozniak et al., 2005); however, KBP has since been shown to interact with a subset of other kinesin family members to regulate diverse cellular processes including mitosis (Brouwers et al., 2017; Malaby et al., 2019), spermatogenesis (Lehti et al., 2015), and neuronal differentiation, growth, and cargo distribution (Alves et al., 2010; Lyons et al., 2008; Drévillon et al., 2013; Drerup et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2019; Hirst et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brouwers et al., 2017; Malaby et al., 2019; Lehti et al., 2015; Alves et al., 2010; Lyons et al., 2008; Drévillon et al., 2013; Drerup et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2019; Hirst et al., 2017.

claim: KBP is a 72 kDa protein.
source: KBP is a 72 kDa protein, is predicted to contain several tetratricopeptide repeats (TPRs), and to be mainly α-helical in secondary structure content (Wozniak et al., 2005; Kevenaar et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wozniak et al., 2005; Kevenaar et al., 2016.

claim: KBP is predicted to contain several tetratricopeptide repeats (TPRs).
source: KBP is a 72 kDa protein, is predicted to contain several tetratricopeptide repeats (TPRs), and to be mainly α-helical in secondary structure content (Wozniak et al., 2005; Kevenaar et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wozniak et al., 2005; Kevenaar et al., 2016.

claim: KBP is predicted to be mainly α-helical in secondary structure content.
source: KBP is a 72 kDa protein, is predicted to contain several tetratricopeptide repeats (TPRs), and to be mainly α-helical in secondary structure content (Wozniak et al., 2005; Kevenaar et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wozniak et al., 2005; Kevenaar et al., 2016.

claim: The 3D structure of KBP at 4.6 Å resolution was determined using cryo-EM data collected using a Volta phase plate.
source: The 3D structure of the ~72 kDa KBP at 4.6 Å resolution (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and b) was determined using cryo-EM data collected using a Volta phase plate (VPP), and an atomic model was calculated (see Materials and methods Table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the manuscript.

claim: KBP is a right-handed α-solenoid protein.
source: Our structure revealed that KBP is a right-handed α-solenoid protein (Figure 1a and b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c–e).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 1.

claim: KBP contains nine pairs of anti-parallel α-helices broken by a single 'linker α-helix' (LαH) and 'linker loop' (LL) in the centre of the fold.
source: Nine pairs of anti-parallel α-helices (αHP1 [α-helical pair 1] to αHP9) are broken by a single 'linker α-helix' (LαH) and 'linker loop' (LL) in the centre of the fold separating KBP into N-terminal and C-terminal subdomains (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1c–e, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: The linker α-helix and linker loop separate KBP into N-terminal and C-terminal subdomains.
source: Nine pairs of anti-parallel α-helices (αHP1 [α-helical pair 1] to αHP9) are broken by a single 'linker α-helix' (LαH) and 'linker loop' (LL) in the centre of the fold separating KBP into N-terminal and C-terminal subdomains (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1c–e, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: The four predicted TPR motifs contribute exclusively to α-helical pairs in the N-terminal subdomain.
source: The four predicted TPR motifs contribute exclusively to α-helical pairs in the N-terminal subdomain (Figure 1a,d, and e).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The structure of KBP alone at 4.6 Å resolution was determined at the 'gold-standard' 0.143 FSC cutoff.
source: Gold-standard Fourier shell correlation (FSC) curves between independent masked, unmasked, phase-randomised, and corrected half-maps (Chen et al., 2013) of KBP as calculated by RELION v3.1 (Zivanov et al., 2018) (4.6 Å resolution at the 'gold-standard' 0.143 FSC cutoff).
evidence: Supported by FSC data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The structure of the KBP–KIF15_MD6S complex was determined at 6.9 Å resolution.
source: To elucidate the mechanism of kinesin inhibition by KBP, we determined the structure of KBP in complex with the human KIF15 (kinesin-12) motor domain (KIF15_MD, 1–375). This construct, which has six of its eight cysteine residues mutated to serine (C5S, C50S, C162S, C294S, C314S, and C346S) and two additional cysteines were inserted (S250C and G375C), has comparable steady-state ATPase activity to previously published reports (Klejnot et al., 2014; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) and we refer to it as KIF15_MD6S. The overall resolution of this KBP–KIF15_MD6S complex was 6.9 Å, with KBP and KIF15_MD6S determined to similar local resolutions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: KIF15_MD6S has comparable steady-state ATPase activity to previously published reports.
source: This construct, which has six of its eight cysteine residues mutated to serine (C5S, C50S, C162S, C294S, C314S, and C346S) and two additional cysteines were inserted (S250C and G375C), has comparable steady-state ATPase activity to previously published reports (Klejnot et al., 2014; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) and we refer to it as KIF15_MD6S.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and citation to Klejnot et al., 2014.

claim: In the KBP–KIF15_MD6S complex, KIF15_MD6S sits in the concave face of the KBP α-solenoid.
source: The complex is arranged such that KIF15_MD6S sits in the concave face of the KBP α-solenoid, analogous to a baseball enclosed in a baseball glove.
evidence: Supported by structural data from the KBP–KIF15_MD6S complex.

claim: The kinesin MD is positioned centrally between the N- and C-terminal subdomains and contacts the KBP concave face and loops at the α-solenoid edges.
source: The kinesin MD is positioned centrally between the N- and C-terminal subdomains and contacts the KBP concave face and loops at the α-solenoid edges.
evidence: Supported by structural data from the KBP–KIF15_MD6S complex.

claim: KBP undergoes a conformational change in the presence of its kinesin motor domain-binding partner, with the largest differences resulting from an unfurling motion of its N-terminal subdomain.
source: When the structure of KBP-alone is superimposed onto KBP in the KBP–KIF15_MD6S complex, it is clear that KBP undergoes a conformational change in the presence of its kinesin motor domain-binding partner, with the largest differences resulting from an unfurling motion of its N-terminal subdomain (Figure 2c and d and Video 1).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2c and d and Video 1.

claim: The KBP-alone model is incompatible with KIF15_MD6S binding due to clashes with L14 in the C-terminal subdomain and αHP3a, αHP4a, and L8 in the N-terminal subdomain.
source: The KBP-alone model is incompatible with KIF15_MD6S binding, due to clashes with L14 in the C-terminal subdomain and αHP3a, αHP4a, and L8 in the N-terminal subdomain.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison and inference from the data.

claim: The conformational changes in KBP upon KIF15_MD6S binding relieve clashes in the complex.
source: The conformational changes in KBP upon KIF15_MD6S binding relieve these clashes in the complex (Video 1).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Video 1.

claim: KIF1A_MD also interacts with KBP on its concave face in the same way as KIF15_MD6S.
source: However, these data did allow us to confirm that indeed KIF1A_MD also interacts with KBP on its concave face in the same way as KIF15_MD6S and suggests a common mechanism of kinesin inhibition by KBP.
evidence: Supported by 2D classification data from KBP–KIF1A_MD complex.

claim: There is a common mechanism of kinesin inhibition by KBP.
source: However, these data did allow us to confirm that indeed KIF1A_MD also interacts with KBP on its concave face in the same way as KIF15_MD6S and suggests a common mechanism of kinesin inhibition by KBP.
evidence: Inferred from structural data of KBP–KIF15_MD6S and KBP–KIF1A_MD complexes.

claim: The structure of the MT-bound, AMPPNP state of KIF15_MD6S was determined, which shows that this MD adopts a canonical conformation.
source: We determined the structure of the MT-bound, AMPPNP state of KIF15_MD6S, which shows that this MD adopts a canonical conformation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: KBP binds the kinesin motor domain via the tubulin-binding subdomain.
source: The structure of the KBP–KIF15_MD6S complex revealed that KBP binds the kinesin motor domain via the tubulin-binding subdomain (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is a striking lack of density in the expected position for helix α4 in the KBP–KIF15_MD6S complex.
source: In particular, there is a striking lack of density in the expected position for helix α4 (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Helix α4 is displaced by ~15 Å into the concave face of KBP in the KBP–KIF15_MD6S complex.
source: Instead, there was a strong density of length and width consistent with helix α4 displaced by ~15 Å into the concave face of KBP, which we modelled as such (Figure 3b and e, Figure 2, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2b–e).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3b and e, Figure 2, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2b–e.

claim: The displacement of helix α4 lies close to the TPR-repeat region of the N-terminal subdomain of KBP.
source: This displacement of helix α4, which lies close to the TPR-repeat region of the N-terminal subdomain of KBP, is accompanied by additional rearrangements of the flanking L11 and L12 in KIF15_MD6S (labelled KL11 and KL12; Figure 3c–e and Figure 3—figure supplement 2b–e).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3c–e and Figure 3—figure supplement 2b–e.

claim: The displacement of helix α4 is accompanied by additional rearrangements of the flanking L11 and L12 in KIF15_MD6S.
source: This displacement of helix α4, which lies close to the TPR-repeat region of the N-terminal subdomain of KBP, is accompanied by additional rearrangements of the flanking L11 and L12 in KIF15_MD6S (labelled KL11 and KL12; Figure 3c–e and Figure 3—figure supplement 2b–e).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3c–e and Figure 3—figure supplement 2b–e.

claim: KBP binds helix α4 of KIF15_MD6S in a similar way to other TPR-containing α-solenoids that bind peptide motifs with α-helical content within their concave faces.
source: A number of other TPR-containing α-solenoids are known to bind peptide motifs with α-helical content within their concave faces (Culurgioni et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2009; Quinaud et al., 2007; Figure 3—figure supplement 3), and our structure shows that KBP binds helix α4 of KIF15_MD6S in a similar way.
evidence: Supported by comparison to other structures cited (Culurgioni et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2009; Quinaud et al., 2007) and structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The KBP-bound conformation of the KIF15_MD6S tubulin-binding subdomain is radically different from its MT-bound conformation.
source: The KBP-bound conformation of the KIF15_MD6S tubulin-binding subdomain is also radically different from its MT-bound conformation (Figure 3d and e).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3d and e.

claim: The tubulin-binding subdomain forms the majority of the MT-binding surface in the KIF15_MD6S-MT complex.
source: The tubulin-binding subdomain forms the majority of the MT-binding surface in the KIF15_MD6S-MT complex (Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) such that KBP and MTs cannot simultaneously bind KIF15_MD6S due to extensive steric overlap (Figure 3d and e).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: KBP and MTs cannot simultaneously bind KIF15_MD6S due to extensive steric overlap.
source: The tubulin-binding subdomain forms the majority of the MT-binding surface in the KIF15_MD6S-MT complex (Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) such that KBP and MTs cannot simultaneously bind KIF15_MD6S due to extensive steric overlap (Figure 3d and e).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3d and e.

claim: KBP sequesters and blocks the MT-interacting surface of kinesin motor domains via a mechanism that involves significant conformational change within the motor domain.
source: In summary, KBP sequesters and blocks the MT-interacting surface of kinesin motor domains via a mechanism that involves significant conformational change within the motor domain.
evidence: Inferred from structural data of KBP–KIF15_MD6S complex.

claim: KBP contacts the KIF15_MD6S both via loops connecting the α-solenoid edges and TPR-containing α-helices at the concave face.
source: KBP contacts the KIF15_MD6S both via (1) loops connecting the α-solenoid edges and (2) TPR-containing α-helices at the concave face (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Video 2).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Video 2.

claim: At the α-solenoid edges, L1, L3, L5, and L10 in the N-terminal subdomain and L12, L14, L16, and L18 in the C-terminal subdomain are close enough to KIF15_MD6S to be involved in binding.
source: At the α-solenoid edges, L1, L3, L5, and L10 in the N-terminal subdomain and L12, L14, L16, and L18 in the C-terminal subdomain are close enough to KIF15_MD6S to be involved in binding.
evidence: Supported by structural data from the KBP–KIF15_MD6S complex.

claim: KBP L12 and L14 contact both Kβ5–KL8 and KL12–Kα5–KL13 regions of the KIF15 tubulin-binding subdomain.
source: The closest interaction of these was KBP L12 and L14, which contact both Kβ5–KL8 and KL12–Kα5–KL13 regions of the KIF15 tubulin-binding subdomain (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 4.

claim: At the TPR-containing region of the concave face of KBP, αHP4a, αHP4b, and αHP5a contact the K11–Kα4–KL12 region of KIF15_MD6S.
source: At the TPR-containing region of the concave face of KBP, αHP4a, αHP4b, and αHP5a contact the K11–Kα4–KL12 region of KIF15_MD6S (Figure 4c and d).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 4c and d.

claim: Ala-substitutions in the TPR-containing α-helices at the KBP concave face (αHP4a and αHP4b) strongly reduced KBP's interaction with both KIF15_MDC and KIF1A_MDC.
source: Ala-substitutions in the TPR-containing α-helices at the KBP concave face (αHP4a and αHP4b), which lie at the heart of the KBP–KIF15_MD6S structural interface, strongly reduced KBP's interaction with both KIF15_MDC and KIF1A_MDC.
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2b and c.

claim: αHP5a mutants had a similar but less pronounced effect on KBP's interaction with KIF15_MDC and KIF1A_MDC compared to αHP4a and αHP4b mutants.
source: αHP5a mutants had a similar but less pronounced effect (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b and c).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2b and c.

claim: Mutation of L1, L3, or L5 in the KBP N-terminal subdomain or L10 or L16 in the C-terminal subdomain has no effect on KBP's interaction with either KIF15_MDC or KIF1A_MDC.
source: In contrast, mutation of L1, L3, or L5 in the KBP N-terminal subdomain or L10 or L16 in the C-terminal subdomain – none of which form directly visualised interactions with KIF15_MD6S in the cryo-EM reconstruction – has no effect on KBP's interaction with either KIF15_MDC or KIF1A_MDC (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b and c).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2b and c.

claim: Mutation of L12 (to some extent) and of L14 (to a greater extent) reduced KBP interaction with KIF15_MDC and KIF1A_MDC.
source: Mutation of L12 (to some extent) and of L14 (to a greater extent) – which contact both Kβ5–KL8 and KL12–Kα5–KL13 – reduced KBP interaction with KIF15_MDC and KIF1A_MDC (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b and c).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2b and c.

claim: Mutation of L12 + L14 additively disrupted the KBP–motor interaction.
source: Mutation of L12 + L14 additively disrupted the KBP–motor interaction, consistent with the structural proximity of these two loops in the kinesin–KBP complex.
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data and structural data.

claim: L10 + L12 and L10 + L14 mutants had weaker interactions with KIF15_MDC/KIF1A_MDC.
source: L10 + L12 and L10 + L14 mutants also had weaker interactions with KIF15_MDC/KIF1A_MDC (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b and c), again pointing to the additive contributions of loops in the KBP C-terminal subdomain to kinesin binding.
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2b and c.

claim: Mutation of L18 appears to enhance the interaction between KBP and both KIF15_MDC and KIF1A_MDC.
source: Strikingly, mutation of L18 appears to enhance the interaction between KBP and both KIF15_MDC and KIF1A_MDC, suggesting that it may somehow contribute to negative regulation of binding in the context of WT KBP.
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data.

claim: Ala-substitutions in the TPR-containing α-helices αHP4a and αHP4b at the KBP concave face, as well as αHP5a, all strongly reduced KBP's inhibition of both KIF15_MDC and KIF1A_MDC peroxisome translocation activity.
source: As with the pull-down assay, Ala-substitutions in the TPR-containing α-helices αHP4a and αHP4b at the KBP concave face, as well as αHP5a, all strongly reduced KBP's inhibition of both KIF15_MDC and KIF1A_MDC peroxisome translocation activity (Figure 5d–g).
evidence: Supported by translocation assay data shown in Figure 5d–g.

claim: Mutation of L1, L3, or L5 had no effect on KBP's inhibition of KIF15_MDC or KIF1A_MDC in the translocation assay.
source: Also, as observed in the pull-down assay, mutation of L1, L3, or L5 had no effect on KBP's inhibition of KIF15_MDC or KIF1A_MDC (Figure 5d–g).
evidence: Supported by translocation assay data shown in Figure 5d–g.

claim: Mutation of either of L12 or L14 strongly abrogated KBP inhibition of KIF15_MDC/KIF1A_MDC-based translocation.
source: Mutation of either of L12 or L14 strongly abrogated KBP inhibition of KIF15_MDC/KIF1A_MDC-based translocation, a more pronounced effect than was seen in the pull-down assay.
evidence: Supported by translocation assay data shown in Figure 5d–g.

claim: Mutation of L10 and L16 disrupted KBP inhibition of KIF1A_MDC and KIF15_MDC in the translocation assay.
source: Similarly, although mutation of L10 and L16 had no effect on KBP–kinesin interaction in the pull-down assay, mutation of these loops disrupted KBP inhibition of KIF1A_MDC and KIF15_MDC in the translocation assay (Figure 5d–g).
evidence: Supported by translocation assay data shown in Figure 5d–g.

claim: The L18 KBP mutant inhibited KIF15_MDC equivalent to wild type, but only exhibited partial inhibition of KIF1A_MDC-mediated translocation.
source: Interestingly, while all the above described regions affected KBP inhibition of KIF15_MDC and KIF1A_MDC equivalently, the L18 KBP mutant inhibited KIF15_MDC equivalent to wild type, but only exhibited partial inhibition of KIF1A_MDC-mediated translocation.
evidence: Supported by translocation assay data.

claim: The translocation and pull-down assays both demonstrate the functional importance of the kinesin interaction with the TPR-containing α-helices at the KBP concave face and the set of loops in the KBP C-terminal subdomain.
source: However, taken together, the translocation and pull-down assays both demonstrate the functional importance of the kinesin interaction with the TPR-containing α-helices at the KBP concave face and the set of loops in the KBP C-terminal subdomain.
evidence: Inferred from combined results of translocation and pull-down assays.

claim: The translocation and pull-down assays reveal differences in the sensitivity of the KBP–kinesin interaction to perturbation, where translocation is more readily disrupted than the interactions detected by pull-down.
source: The translocation and pull-down assays also reveal differences in the sensitivity of the KBP–kinesin interaction to perturbation, where translocation is more readily disrupted than the interactions detected by pull-down.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of translocation and pull-down assay results.

claim: KBP interacts with different kinesin family members in a similar way via an extended interface at KBP's concave face that is composed of TPR-containing α-helices and α-solenoid edge loops, particularly in the C-terminal subdomain.
source: Overall, these mutation studies support the idea that KBP interacts with different kinesin family members in a similar way via an extended interface at KBP's concave face that is composed of TPR-containing α-helices and α-solenoid edge loops, particularly in the C-terminal subdomain.
evidence: Inferred from mutation studies and structural data.

claim: Analysis of the sequences of the tubulin-binding subdomain in KBP-binding and KBP-non-binding kinesins revealed patterns of sequence conservation across the entire subdomain in all KBP-binding kinesins.
source: Analysis of the sequences of this region in KBP-binding and KBP-non-binding kinesins (Figure 6a) revealed patterns of sequence conservation across the entire subdomain in all KBP-binding kinesins; this included both the Kβ5–KL8 and KL11–Kα4–KL12–Kα5–KL13 regions.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The equivalent regions are more variable in kinesins that are not inhibited by KBP.
source: In contrast, the equivalent regions are more variable in kinesins that are not inhibited by KBP.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The length of KL8 was consistently five residues long in KBP-binding kinesins, while it was variable in KBP-non-binding kinesins.
source: The length of KL8, which joins the two Kβ5 strands, was also consistently five residues long in KBP-binding kinesins, while it was variable in KBP-non-binding kinesins.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The sensitivity of the KBP interaction to KL8 length makes sense considering the tight fit of this loop between KBP L12 and L14.
source: From our KBP–KIF15_MD6S structure, the sensitivity of the KBP interaction to KL8 length makes sense considering the tight fit of this loop between KBP L12 and L14 (Figure 6b).
evidence: Inferred from structural data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Two consensus motifs in KL11–Kα4–KL12–Kα5–KL13 and Kβ5–KL8 regions of the tubulin-binding subdomain are found in KBP-binding kinesins and these are likely to form the basis of KBP's kinesin family member selectivity.
source: In summary, two consensus motifs in KL11–Kα4–KL12–Kα5–KL13 and Kβ5–KL8 regions of the tubulin-binding subdomain are found in KBP-binding kinesins and these are likely to form the basis of KBP's kinesin family member selectivity.
evidence: Inferred from sequence analysis and structural data.

claim: KBP selects and inhibits target kinesins through binding and remodelling a compatible tubulin-binding subdomain, obstructing the kinesin MT-binding surface.
source: We therefore propose a model where KBP selects and inhibits target kinesins through binding and remodelling a compatible tubulin-binding subdomain, obstructing the kinesin MT-binding surface (Figure 6c).
evidence: Proposed model based on structural and functional data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: At the time of writing, structures of only a few macromolecular complexes <80 kDa have been determined using cryo-EM.
source: At the time of writing and to our knowledge, structures of only a few macromolecular complexes <80 kDa have been determined using cryo-EM (Merk et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018; Khoshouei et al., 2017; Herzik et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Merk et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018; Khoshouei et al., 2017; Herzik et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2019.

claim: The structure of the KBP–KIF15_MD6S complex shows how KBP binds the KIF15_MD6S via its concave face and undergoes subtle remodelling of its N-terminal domain to accommodate kinesin binding.
source: The structure of the KBP–KIF15_MD6S complex shows how KBP binds the KIF15_MD6S via its concave face and undergoes subtle remodelling of its N-terminal domain to accommodate kinesin binding.
evidence: Supported by structural data from the KBP–KIF15_MD6S complex.

claim: TPR-containing structures are not simply static scaffolds but can flexibly respond to ligand binding.
source: This further reinforces the idea that the TPR-containing structures are not simply static scaffolds but can flexibly respond to ligand binding (Pernigo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pernigo et al., 2018 and structural data from this study.

claim: The KIF15 motor domain undergoes a radical conformational change in forming a complex with KBP, in which helix α4 is displaced from the main MD body by ~15 Å into the KBP concave face.
source: In contrast, the KIF15 motor domain undergoes a radical conformational change in forming a complex with KBP, in which helix α4, the major component of the motor's tubulin-binding subdomain, is displaced from the main MD body by ~15 Å into the KBP concave face.
evidence: Supported by structural data from the KBP–KIF15_MD6S complex.

claim: The region of the kinesin motor domain containing helix α4 is rather malleable and able to move independently of the core structure of kinesin motor domains.
source: This is consistent with previous observations that this region of the kinesin motor domain being rather malleable and able to move independently of the core structure of kinesin motor domains (Wang et al., 2016a; Scarabelli and Grant, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2016a and Scarabelli and Grant, 2013.

claim: The large displacement of helix α4 expands the surface area over which the normally compact tubulin-binding subdomain of the kinesin motor domain can interact with KBP.
source: The large displacement of helix α4 expands the surface area over which the normally compact tubulin-binding subdomain of the kinesin motor domain can interact with KBP, and it is through the sequence and shape of this interface that the selectivity of KBP for a subset of kinesin motors is presumably defined.
evidence: Inferred from structural data.

claim: The selectivity of KBP for a subset of kinesin motors is presumably defined through the sequence and shape of the interface between the tubulin-binding subdomain and KBP.
source: The large displacement of helix α4 expands the surface area over which the normally compact tubulin-binding subdomain of the kinesin motor domain can interact with KBP, and it is through the sequence and shape of this interface that the selectivity of KBP for a subset of kinesin motors is presumably defined.
evidence: Inferred from structural and sequence data.

claim: KBP binds exclusively to the tubulin-binding subdomain of KIF15_MD6S, sterically preventing MT attachment.
source: Our structure shows that KBP binds exclusively to the tubulin-binding subdomain of KIF15_MD6S, sterically preventing MT attachment.
evidence: Supported by structural data from the KBP–KIF15_MD6S complex.

claim: The interaction of kinesin motor domains with the MT surface via its tubulin-binding subdomain stimulates nucleotide exchange and kinesin ATPase activity.
source: The interaction of kinesin motor domains with the MT surface via its tubulin-binding subdomain stimulates nucleotide exchange and kinesin ATPase activity.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of kinesin motor domain function.

claim: On interaction with KBP, the displacement of helix α4 from the kinesin nucleotide-binding site, together with the absence of MT-mediated ordering of KL9 and KL11, means that its catalytic site is distorted and the structural changes associated with MT-stimulated ATPase cannot occur.
source: In contrast, on interaction with KBP, the displacement of helix α4 from the kinesin nucleotide-binding site, together with the absence of MT-mediated ordering of KL9 and KL11, means that its catalytic site is distorted and the structural changes associated with MT-stimulated ATPase cannot occur.
evidence: Inferred from structural data of the KBP–KIF15_MD6S complex.

claim: The distortion of the kinesin catalytic site upon KBP binding could be an important facet of the role of KBP in the energy economy of the cell in addition to directly blocking kinesin–MT interactions.
source: This could be an important facet of the role of KBP in the energy economy of the cell in addition to directly blocking kinesin–MT interactions.
evidence: Speculative inference based on structural data.

claim: The concave face of TPR-containing α-solenoids commonly serve as a recognition platform for specific peptide motifs, including those forming α-helical structures.
source: The concave face of TPR-containing α-solenoids commonly serve as a recognition platform for specific peptide motifs, including those forming α-helical structures (Perez-Riba and Itzhaki, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perez-Riba and Itzhaki, 2019.

claim: Specificity and affinity for target motifs in TPR-containing α-solenoids are determined in part by the shape of the α-solenoid concave face, which in turn is defined by the fold's supertwist.
source: Specificity and affinity for target motifs are determined in part by the shape of the α-solenoid concave face, which in turn is defined by the fold's supertwist.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of TPR-containing α-solenoid structures.

claim: Particular amino acid arrangements at the concave face contribute to partner-binding affinity and specificity in TPR-containing α-solenoids, together with additional interfaces formed at the convex surface or α-solenoid edge.
source: In addition, particular amino acid arrangements at the concave face contribute to partner-binding affinity and specificity, together with additional interfaces formed at the convex surface or α-solenoid edge (Zeytuni and Zarivach, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zeytuni and Zarivach, 2012.

claim: KBP kinesin specificity and affinity are defined by the interaction of its concave face with the large surface area of the kinesin L11–Kα4–KL12–Kα5–KL13 region, in addition to binding the kinesin Kβ5–KL8 region at its α-solenoid edge.
source: KBP kinesin specificity and affinity are defined by the interaction of its concave face with the large surface area of the kinesin L11–Kα4–KL12–Kα5–KL13 region, in addition to binding the kinesin Kβ5–KL8 region at its α-solenoid edge.
evidence: Inferred from structural data of the KBP–KIF15_MD6S complex.

claim: Distal to the N-terminal MT-binding region of kinesin-1, C-terminally associated kinesin light chain use their unique TPR-containing α-solenoid concave face to select cargos via recognition of specific peptide motifs.
source: Interestingly, distal to the N-terminal MT-binding region of kinesin-1, C-terminally associated kinesin light chain use their unique TPR-containing α-solenoid concave face to select cargos via recognition of specific peptide motifs (Cross and Dodding, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cross and Dodding, 2019.

claim: Peptide selectivity by TPR-containing α-solenoids is a facet of both kinesin MT-binding and cargo-binding regulatory mechanisms.
source: Therefore, peptide selectivity by TPR-containing α-solenoids is a facet of both kinesin MT-binding and cargo-binding regulatory mechanisms.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of KBP function and kinesin light chain function.

claim: Protein–protein interactions involving TPR-containing α-solenoids may be selectively targeted for disruption.
source: Such protein–protein interactions may be selectively targeted for disruption (Randall et al., 2017), and the insights arising from our work provide future avenues to disrupt KBP–kinesin interactions and thereby explore KBP interactions and regulatory roles.
evidence: Supported by citation to Randall et al., 2017 and speculative inference.

claim: The insights arising from this work provide future avenues to disrupt KBP–kinesin interactions and thereby explore KBP interactions and regulatory roles.
source: Such protein–protein interactions may be selectively targeted for disruption (Randall et al., 2017), and the insights arising from our work provide future avenues to disrupt KBP–kinesin interactions and thereby explore KBP interactions and regulatory roles.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the structural and functional data presented.

claim: The effective and selective kinesin inhibitory mechanism of KBP revealed by this work may fulfil specific roles in the kinesin regulatory toolbox employed by cells to spatially and temporarily orchestrate kinesin activity.
source: The effective and selective kinesin inhibitory mechanism of KBP revealed by our work may fulfil specific roles in the kinesin regulatory toolbox employed by cells to spatially and temporarily orchestrate kinesin activity.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the structural and functional data presented.

claim: KBP does not interact with some target kinesins in autoinhibited conformations.
source: For example, while KBP does not interact with some target kinesins in autoinhibited conformations (Malaby et al., 2019), others that retain a structurally available tubulin-binding subdomain, such as autoinhibited kinesin-3 monomers (Ren et al., 2018), are feasible binding partners.
evidence: Supported by citation to Malaby et al., 2019.

claim: Autoinhibited kinesin-3 monomers that retain a structurally available tubulin-binding subdomain are feasible KBP binding partners.
source: For example, while KBP does not interact with some target kinesins in autoinhibited conformations (Malaby et al., 2019), others that retain a structurally available tubulin-binding subdomain, such as autoinhibited kinesin-3 monomers (Ren et al., 2018), are feasible binding partners.
evidence: Inferred from citation to Ren et al., 2018 and structural data.

claim: KBP can bind to constitutively active dimeric kinesin constructs that lack autoinhibitory regions.
source: KBP can bind to constitutively active dimeric kinesin constructs that lack autoinhibitory regions (Kevenaar et al., 2016; Malaby et al., 2019), although the stoichiometry and structural details in this context are unclear.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kevenaar et al., 2016 and Malaby et al., 2019.

claim: The stoichiometry and structural details of KBP binding to constitutively active dimeric kinesin constructs are unclear.
source: KBP can bind to constitutively active dimeric kinesin constructs that lack autoinhibitory regions (Kevenaar et al., 2016; Malaby et al., 2019), although the stoichiometry and structural details in this context are unclear.
evidence: Acknowledged gap in knowledge.

claim: KBP activity can be regulated by phosphorylation of KBP and/or kinesins.
source: It will also be of key importance to elucidate the mechanisms of KBP activity regulation, for example, by phosphorylation of KBP and/or kinesins (Kevenaar et al., 2016) and KBP acetylation and targeted degradation by the ubiquitin system (Donato et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kevenaar et al., 2016.

claim: KBP activity can be regulated by KBP acetylation and targeted degradation by the ubiquitin system.
source: It will also be of key importance to elucidate the mechanisms of KBP activity regulation, for example, by phosphorylation of KBP and/or kinesins (Kevenaar et al., 2016) and KBP acetylation and targeted degradation by the ubiquitin system (Donato et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Donato et al., 2017.

claim: The structural characterisation of the KBP–kinesin inhibitory interaction provides an important mechanistic platform from which to expand understanding of KBP's biological roles in neuronal function and cancer.
source: Our structural characterisation of the KBP–kinesin inhibitory interaction provides an important mechanistic platform from which to expand our understanding of KBP's biological roles in neuronal function and cancer.
evidence: Inferred from the structural and functional data presented.
